entries.rule: Address superiors by their rank and last name, using 'mon' or 'madame' for officers.

examples.situation: Liaison meeting with a French Air Force colonel.
examples.say: 'Colonel Dupont, voici les informations que vous avez demandées.'
examples.dontSay: 'Colonel, voici les informations que vous avez demandées.'
examples.why: Omitting 'Dupont' is disrespectful as it lacks personal address.

examples.situation: Briefing with a French Air and Space Force general.
examples.say: 'Général Martin, nous sommes prêts à commencer.'
examples.dontSay: 'Général, nous sommes prêts à commencer.'
examples.why: Omitting 'Martin' is disrespectful as it lacks personal address.

entries.rule: Address peers by their rank and last name, or simply by their last name if the relationship is informal.

examples.situation: Office visit with a French Air Force captain.
examples.say: 'Capitaine Bernard, comment allez-vous?' or 'Bernard, comment allez-vous?'
examples.dontSay: 'Capitaine, comment ça va?'
examples.why: Using 'ça va' is too casual and informal for a professional setting.

examples.situation: Meal with French Air and Space Force counterparts.
examples.say: 'Lieutenant Moreau, passez-moi le pain, s’il vous plaît.'
examples.dontSay: 'Moreau, passe le pain.'
examples.why: Using the informal 'passe' is inappropriate without prior invitation to do so.

source.doc: general knowledge — no AFCLC field guide for France

entries.rule: Address civilians by their title and last name, such as 'Monsieur' or 'Madame'.

examples.situation: Gate meeting with a French contractor.
examples.say: 'Monsieur Lefèvre, merci d’être venu.'
examples.dontSay: 'Lefèvre, merci d’être venu.'
examples.why: Omitting 'Monsieur' is disrespectful as it lacks proper title.

examples.situation: Briefing with a French government official.
examples.say: 'Madame Dubois, voici notre rapport.'
examples.dontSay: 'Dubois, voici notre rapport.'
examples.why: Omitting 'Madame' is disrespectful as it lacks proper title.

entries.rule: When refusing a request or offer, French speakers often use indirect language and polite phrases to soften the refusal.

examples.situation: A liaison meeting where you are asked to provide sensitive information that you cannot share.
examples.say: Je suis désolé, mais je ne suis pas autorisé à partager ces informations pour le moment.
examples.dontSay: Je ne peux pas vous donner ces informations.
examples.why: The direct refusal may come across as abrupt and uncooperative.

examples.situation: A meal with French counterparts where you are offered a type of food you are allergic to.
examples.say: C'est très gentil, mais je pense que je vais devoir passer mon tour à cause d'une allergie.
examples.dontSay: Je ne peux pas manger ça.
examples.why: The direct refusal may seem rude and ungrateful for the offer.

source.doc: general knowledge — no AFCLC field guide for France

entries.rule: French speakers may use conditional tense or phrases like 'peut-être' (maybe) or 'je ne sais pas' (I don't know) to indicate refusal indirectly.

examples.situation: At a gate, a French soldier asks if you can help them with a task that is outside your responsibility.
examples.say: Je ne suis pas sûr que ce soit dans mes attributions, mais je peux demander à quelqu'un d'autre.
examples.dontSay: Ce n'est pas mon travail.
examples.why: The direct refusal may seem dismissive and unhelpful.

examples.situation: During a briefing, you are asked to commit to a deadline that you know is not feasible.
examples.say: Peut-être pourrions-nous envisager une date un peu plus tardive?
examples.dontSay: Nous ne pouvons pas respecter cette date.
examples.why: The direct refusal may come across as uncooperative and inflexible.

source.doc: general knowledge — no AFCLC field guide for France

entries.rule: When refusing, it is important to provide a reason or alternative to maintain a positive relationship.

examples.situation: In an office visit, a French colleague asks you to attend a social event that conflicts with your schedule.
examples.say: Malheureusement, j'ai déjà un engagement ce soir-là, mais j'espère que nous pourrons se voir une autre fois.
examples.dontSay: Je ne peux pas venir.
examples.why: The direct refusal may seem uncaring and dismissive of the invitation.

examples.situation: A French civilian asks for a favor that you cannot accommodate due to military regulations.
examples.say: Je suis vraiment désolé, mais en raison des règlements, je ne peux pas faire cela. Peut-être pourrions-nous trouver une autre solution?
examples.dontSay: Les règlements m'empêchent de faire ça.
examples.why: The direct refusal may come across as cold and unapproachable.

entries.rule: When apologizing, be specific about what you're apologizing for and express genuine remorse. In formal settings, use 'Je m'excuse' instead of the more casual 'Désolé'.

examples.situation: Liaison meeting, you're late
examples.say: Je m'excuse pour mon retard. C'était inattendu.
examples.dontSay: Désolé pour le retard.
examples.why: The casual 'Désolé' is inappropriate in a formal meeting.

examples.situation: Office visit, you've made a mistake in a report
examples.say: Je m'excuse pour l'erreur dans le rapport. Je vais le corriger immédiatement.
examples.dontSay: C'est pas grave, c'est juste une petite erreur.
examples.why: Downplaying the mistake is not a proper apology.

source.doc: general knowledge — no AFCLC field guide for France

entries.rule: When thanking someone, be specific about what you're thanking them for and use 'Merci beaucoup' for a stronger expression of gratitude.

examples.situation: Gate, a French counterpart holds the door open for you
examples.say: Merci beaucoup pour votre aide.
examples.dontSay: Merci.
examples.why: A simple 'Merci' may seem less appreciative.

examples.situation: Briefing, a French colleague provides helpful information
examples.say: Merci beaucoup pour ces informations utiles.
examples.dontSay: C'est bon, j'ai compris.
examples.why: Acknowledging the help is important.

source.doc: general knowledge — no AFCLC field guide for France

entries.rule: With civilians, use polite forms and avoid military jargon. For apologies, 'Je m'excuse' is still preferred, and for thanks, 'Merci beaucoup' is appropriate.

examples.situation: Meal with counterparts, a civilian host prepares a traditional French meal
examples.say: Je m'excuse si nous avons des manières différentes. Merci beaucoup pour ce délicieux repas.
examples.dontSay: Désolé si on mange comme des animaux. Merci pour la bouffe.
examples.why: The casual language and expressions are inappropriate with civilians.

examples.situation: Gate, a civilian security guard assists you
examples.say: Merci beaucoup pour votre aide, monsieur.
examples.dontSay: Merci, soldat.
examples.why: Using 'soldat' for a civilian is incorrect and disrespectful.

entries.rule: Avoid discussing personal relationships or family matters, as it can be seen as intrusive.

examples.situation: Liaison meeting with French Air and Space Force officers.
examples.say: Quel temps magnifique aujourd'hui, n'est-ce pas?
examples.dontSay: Alors, vous êtes marié? Vous avez des enfants?
examples.why: The French generally prefer to keep personal life separate from professional life.

examples.situation: Office visit with a French colleague.
examples.say: Avez-vous des projets pour le week-end?
examples.dontSay: Alors, comment va votre femme? Elle est en bonne santé?
examples.why: Asking about a colleague's spouse can be seen as too personal.

source.doc: general knowledge — no AFCLC field guide for France

entries.rule: Do not bring up sensitive political topics such as France's colonial past or current immigration policies.

examples.situation: Briefing with French Air and Space Force and NATO allies.
examples.say: La météo semble claire pour les opérations aujourd'hui.
examples.dontSay: Qu'en pensez-vous de la politique d'immigration actuelle en France?
examples.why: Political topics can be divisive and are best avoided in a professional setting.

examples.situation: Meal with French counterparts.
examples.say: Ce vin est excellent. Quelle est la région d'origine?
examples.dontSay: Alors, que pensez-vous de la décision de Macron sur...?
examples.why: Discussing political decisions can lead to uncomfortable conversations.

source.doc: general knowledge — no AFCLC field guide for France

entries.rule: Avoid discussing salary or financial matters, as it is considered impolite.

examples.situation: Gate meeting with French Air and Space Force personnel.
examples.say: Avez-vous des recommandations pour des endroits à visiter à Paris?
examples.dontSay: Combien gagnez-vous ici? Le salaire est-il bon?
examples.why: Financial discussions are private and not appropriate for small talk.

examples.situation: Liaison meeting with French Air and Space Force officers.
examples.say: Le café ici est très bon. Vous en voulez une autre tasse?
examples.dontSay: Quel est votre salaire annuel? Je suis juste curieux.
examples.why: Inquiring about someone's salary is seen as nosy and impolite.

source.doc: general knowledge — no AFCLC field guide for France

entries.rule: Express disagreement politely and respectfully, using indirect language and softening phrases.

examples.situation: Liaison meeting discussing logistics
examples.say: Je ne suis pas tout à fait d'accord, peut-être pourrions-nous envisager une autre approche?
examples.dontSay: Votre idée est mauvaise, ça ne marchera pas.
examples.why: The direct and harsh language is likely to offend and escalate tension.

examples.situation: Briefing with French Air and Space Force counterparts
examples.say: Je vois votre point, cependant, je pense que nous devrions considérer les aspects suivants...
examples.dontSay: Vous avez tort, écoutez-moi.
examples.why: The direct contradiction and interruption are considered rude in French culture.

source.doc: general knowledge — no AFCLC field guide for France

entries.rule: Avoid direct confrontation and maintain a collaborative tone.

examples.situation: Office visit discussing joint operations
examples.say: Je comprends votre perspective, mais peut-être pourrions-nous trouver un compromis?
examples.dontSay: Non, c'est stupide, nous devons faire à ma façon.
examples.why: The dismissive language and lack of willingness to compromise are inappropriate.

examples.situation: Meeting with local civilians discussing base expansion
examples.say: Je vois vos préoccupations, mais pourrions-nous discuter des avantages potentiels?
examples.dontSay: Vos inquiétudes sont sans importance, nous allons faire cela de toute façon.
examples.why: The dismissive attitude and lack of consideration for local concerns are disrespectful.

source.doc: general knowledge — no AFCLC field guide for France

entries.rule: Use questions and suggestions to express disagreement, keeping the conversation open and respectful.

examples.situation: Gate meeting discussing security protocols
examples.say: Avez-vous envisagé les implications de cette approche? Peut-être pourrions-nous explorer d'autres options?
examples.dontSay: Cette idée est ridicule, elle ne fonctionnera jamais.
examples.why: The direct insult and dismissive language are inappropriate and offensive.

examples.situation: Meal with French counterparts discussing cultural differences
examples.say: C'est intéressant, mais comment pourrions-nous concilier nos différentes approches?
examples.dontSay: Vous vous trompez, notre façon est la bonne.
examples.why: The direct contradiction and assumption of superiority are disrespectful and uncooperative.

entries.rule: Accept invitations to meals or social events when extended by French counterparts, as it is a sign of respect and fosters good relations.

examples.situation: A French officer invites you to dinner at their home after a liaison meeting.
examples.say: Avec plaisir, merci pour l'invitation.
examples.dontSay: Je ne peux pas, je dois travailler.
examples.why: Declining the invitation might be seen as rejecting their hospitality and could harm the relationship.

examples.situation: You are invited to join French colleagues for coffee during an office visit.
examples.say: Volontiers, merci.
examples.dontSay: Non, merci. Je n'aime pas le café.
examples.why: Even if you don't like coffee, declining could be seen as rude; you can simply not drink it.

source.doc: general knowledge — no AFCLC field guide for France

entries.rule: Offer to reciprocate hospitality when appropriate, such as inviting French counterparts to a meal or event hosted by US service members.

examples.situation: During a briefing, a French officer mentions they enjoy trying new foods.
examples.say: Nous organisons un barbecue la semaine prochaine, vous seriez les bienvenus.
examples.dontSay: Nous avons beaucoup de nourriture aux États-Unis.
examples.why: The first sentence extends a genuine invitation, while the second is merely stating a fact and does not reciprocate hospitality.

examples.situation: After a successful collaboration, you want to thank your French counterparts.
examples.say: Merci pour votre aide. Nous aimerions vous inviter à un dîner pour vous remercier.
examples.dontSay: Merci pour votre aide. Nous avons terminé notre mission.
examples.why: The first response shows appreciation and reciprocates hospitality, while the second only expresses completion of the mission.

source.doc: general knowledge — no AFCLC field guide for France

entries.rule: When interacting with local civilians, be polite and accept small gestures of hospitality, such as offers of coffee or pastries, as a sign of respect for their culture.

examples.situation: A local civilian offers you a croissant during a gate visit.
examples.say: Merci beaucoup, c'est très gentil.
examples.dontSay: Non, merci. Je ne mange pas de petits déjeuners.
examples.why: Declining the offer might be seen as impolite, as it is a small gesture of hospitality.

examples.situation: A shop owner offers you a cup of coffee while you are making a purchase.
examples.say: Avec plaisir, merci.
examples.dontSay: Non, merci. Je dois y aller.
examples.why: Accepting the coffee shows appreciation for their hospitality, while declining might be seen as rude.

source.doc: general knowledge — no AFCLC field guide for France

entries.rule: Avoid using the OK gesture (thumb and index finger forming a circle) as it is considered vulgar in France.

examples.situation: Liaison meeting with French Air and Space Force counterparts
examples.say: C'est correct.
examples.dontSay: Faites le geste OK.
examples.why: The OK gesture is offensive in France.

examples.situation: Briefing with NATO French-speaking allies
examples.say: Tout est en ordre.
examples.dontSay: Montrez le signe de OK.
examples.why: The OK gesture can be seen as rude.

source.doc: general knowledge — no AFCLC field guide for France

entries.rule: Use silence judiciously, as the French may interpret excessive silence as a lack of interest or agreement.

examples.situation: Office visit with a French Armée de l'air et de l'espace officer
examples.say: Je réfléchis à ce que vous avez dit.
examples.dontSay: Restez silencieux pendant une longue période.
examples.why: Silence may be interpreted as disagreement or disinterest.

examples.situation: Meal with French civilian counterparts
examples.say: Je trouve cela intéressant, laissez-moi un moment pour réfléchir.
examples.dontSay: Ne dites rien pendant un long moment.
examples.why: Prolonged silence can make the French uncomfortable.

entries.rule: Avoid the

examples.situation: Gate meeting with French security forces
examples.say: Pouvez-vous répéter, s'il vous plaît?
examples.dontSay: Faites le geste de corne avec votre main.
examples.why: The horn gesture is considered rude in France.

examples.situation: Briefing with French Air and Space Force personnel
examples.say: Je ne comprends pas, pourriez-vous clarifier?
examples.dontSay: Utilisez le geste de corne.
examples.why: This gesture is associated with superstitions and can be offensive.
